title: Nord Stream sabotage trial is getting underway. Here’s a refresher | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

It started with a stream of bubbles rising to the surface of the Baltic Sea.

Seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, explosions burst throughtwo Nord Stream gas pipelines– Russia’s controversial gas highway into Europe – in the waters between Sweden and Poland.

Investigators from several countries raced to determine who was responsible and fingers were immediately pointed at Russia. Then, two Ukrainian nationals were arrested, raising questions about state involvement and presenting a test of loyalty for some of Kyiv’s European allies.

On Wednesday, one of them will go on trial in Germany accused of involvement in one of the biggest – and most mysterious – acts of sabotage in modern history. He denies wrongdoing and Ukraine has denied any involvement.

Here’s what you need to know:

Nord Stream 1 and 2 are two major conduits created to funnel Russian gas to Europe, via Germany.

Owned by Nord Stream AG, whose majority shareholder is the Russian gas firm Gazprom, the pipelines were divisive even before the start of the Ukraine war, mainly due to concerns over European reliance on cheap Russian hydrocarbons.

Nord Stream 1 was announced in 1997, when relations between the West and post-Soviet Russia were relatively calm, and became operational in 2011. Nord Stream 2, a sister project, was completed in September 2021, but never entered service. Germanyshelved itdays before Moscow invaded Ukraine.

In late September 2022, explosions ripped through the two pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm, releasing plumes of gas into the surrounding water and sparking a cross-border investigation.

Sweden was the first country to sound the alarm on the leaks.

Some experts at the time said they could have been caused by a technical malfunction, but the leaders of several Western countries were quick to identifysabotageas the likely cause.

Two months after the event, Swedish prosecutors announced the incident was a result of “gross sabotage,” adding that “traces of explosives” had been found at the scene.

Although neither pipeline was in operation at the time of the attack, both still contained gas under pressure. As a result, experts said an “unprecedented” amount of the greenhouse gases might have leaked into the atmosphere.

Several agencies were tasked with digging into the attack, including German, Danish and Scandinavian security authorities. European officials vowed a firm response.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said any deliberate act to disrupt Europe’s energy infrastructure was “unacceptable” and would “lead to the strongest response possible.”

Germany in particular was keen to see the alleged culprits brought to justice and, in 2024, authorities there issued aninternational arrest warrantfor a Ukrainian man suspected of involvement.

Since then, two Ukrainian men have been arrested over their alleged role in the pipeline attacks.

Denmark and Sweden both closed their criminal investigations into the explosions in 2024, with Sweden citing a lack of jurisdiction and Denmark saying there were not sufficient grounds to pursue the case. This left Berlin the only nation to pursue the leads.

Serhii Kuznietsov, aformer Ukrainian soldier, is the lone defendant in the trial starting Wednesday in Hamburg, where he is identified only as Serhii K under German privacy laws.

German prosecutors said he “belongs to a group of people who planted explosive devices in the gas pipelines Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 near the island of Bornholm in September 2022.”

Prosecutors have accused Serhii K of being an accomplice to the “war crime” of attacking civilian objects, destruction of infrastructure, causing an explosion and disrupting public operations, according to court filings.

The court filings accused him of “acting on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities” in an alleged plot to destroy the Nord Stream pipelines.

His defense lawyer previously told CNN that he denies any wrongdoing.

In 2025, Kuznietsov wasarrestedby Italian police in Rimini – a city in northern Italy known for its sandy beaches and Roman landmarks – and later extradited to Germany.

Prosecutors in Germany believe he and his accomplices used a sailing yacht to carry out the attack, traveling from the port of Rostock, a city in northern Germany. The vessel had been rented from a German company via intermediaries using forged identity documents, prosecutors claim.

The second Ukrainian man arrested in connection with the bombing, Volodymyr Zhuravlov, was detained in August in Croatia, where a court has approved his extradition to Germany, Reuters reported last month. His lawyer dismissed the ruling and said he could appeal the decision, Reuters added.

German prosecutors said he was “strongly suspected” of several criminal offenses, including sabotage and causing an explosion, and participating in dives to the pipelines.

Zhuravlov was previously arrested in Poland, which declined to extradite him to Germany.

The explosions rang out at a tense time for Europe.

The attacks heightened the controversy over Europe’s use of Russian gas and put Germany – the driving force behind the gas project – under the spotlight over former chancellor Angela Merkel’s decision to adopt a conciliatory approach to Moscow despite its recent aggression toward Ukraine and Georgia.

Donald Tusk, the prime minister of Ukraine’s close ally Poland, said last year that Europe’s problem was “not that Nord Stream 2 was blown up, but that it was built.”

As far back as 2007, Poland’s then-defense minister Radek Sikorski railed against the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, then under construction, calling it “the most outrageous attempt by Mr Putin to divide and damage the EU.”

When Zhuravlov was initially arrested in Poland, a judge ruled against his extradition to Germany, saying that if the Nord Stream blasts were an act of Ukrainian sabotage, it would be a justified response to an unprovoked invasion.

With court officials saying Wednesday’s trial is expected to run until February next year, Germany will be hoping no new roadblocks lie ahead as it seeks to get to the truth of this murky affair.

CNN’s Sebastian Shukla, Sophie Tanno, Ivana Kottasová, Chris Liakos, Joseph Ataman, Christian Edwards and Rob Picheta contributed reporting.
